newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Conservative NZ budget seen diluting Peters' clout.
newsitem.headline: Conservative NZ budget seen diluting Peters' clout.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters' budget on Thursday spooned heavy doses of welfare and education spending, but it was the return to market reform which was more important, political analysts said.
New Zealand's centre-right government is a coalition of the conservative National Party and the nationalist New Zealand First Party, which Peters leads.
"It's a National Party budget...The social spending issues are side issues rather than central ones," political commentator Colin James said.
The populist Peters campaigned heavily in last year's election on the need for greater social spending.
And his budget fulfils those promises with projections of NZ$5 billion (US$3.4 billion) in new spending over three years largely in welfare, health and education.
While Peters projected a sharply lower surplus of NZ$1.5 billion against the previous forecast of NZ$3.3 billion, he showed enough fiscal restraint to ensure no selloff in financial markets.
Margaret Clark, politics professor at Wellington's Victoria University, said the budget had a strong stress on fiscal rectitude and the work ethic.
"He wanted to calm the markets, and secondly he wanted to hold his support, such as it is," she said.
Six months ago Peters was riding high, having won the balance of power with the 17 seats won in the October election, and as kingmaker he sided with the ruling conservative National Party.
That upset many of his constituency, the elderly, Maori and beneficiaries who would have preferred Peters to side with the left-leaning Labour Party.
Peters extracted a high price from National, winning eight cabinet seats including the key finance portfolio for himself plus big concessions on social policy.

But Peters and his party have dug themselves into a hole via a series of scandals. Peters assaulted a fellow government member of parliament in the House and was involved in an early morning fracas in a cafe.
NZ First's popularity has slumped from 13 percent support at the election to less than four percent in the latest polls.
Now, above all he must avoid an election before the scheduled date of 1999 where NZ First would be decimated.
And that is seen as the reason why Peters has backed down on his stringent election campaign promises to stop the government's charge down the free market track.

Promises to halt privatisations have been reversed in this budget and his campaign stance against opening the economy to foreigners also lay in tatters with a pledge to accelerate the reduction and removal of tariffs.
James said Peters had to keep the coalition together by making concessions in the cabinet and must hope to fight another day.
"They have given away this year.

"The politics of it is for New Zealand First potentially laying a platform to ride off the back of a big fiscal boost next year, with spending in 1999 which they will try to make (their own) to campaign on," James said.
Clark said Peters may just have done enough on the spending front, including the scrapping of a hated tax surcharge on pensions, to help him survive.
"It will for the foreseeable future save the coalition. But Peters' leverage is very much diminished," she said.
